item.title: Could You Spot Cancer Before the Signs Get Loud?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Cancer is one of the most common health challenges in dogs and cats, affecting roughly 1 in 4 dogs and 1 in 5 cats in their lifetime, with early detection making a dramatic difference in treatment outcomes
  • Warning signs include lumps or bumps that change in size, unexplained weight loss, persistent bad breath, swollen lymph nodes, difficulty breathing or urinating, lameness, and any behavioral change that lingers
  • The most common cancers to know about are lymphoma, mast cell tumors, osteosarcoma (bone cancer in large breeds), melanoma, and mammary tumors, each with distinct early patterns worth having on your radar
  • A monthly five-minute home exam builds a baseline that helps you catch changes much sooner
  • Prevention stacks the odds: a species-appropriate diet, lean body weight, reduced environmental toxins, filtered water, sun protection for light-colored pets, stress management, and integrative supplementation

Cancer is one of the most common health challenges in canine and feline animal companions today, and one of the leading causes of death in both species. In fact, 1 in 4 dogs and 1 in 5 cats will face cancer in their lives. And yet, with early detection, better treatment options than ever, and proactive care, many pets can overcome it or live longer, better lives after a diagnosis.

November is Pet Cancer Awareness Month, making it the perfect time to raise awareness about this disease — not to scare pet parents, but to help them learn the quiet early signals your pet can't put into words. Because here's the harder truth: By the time most cancer diagnoses get made, the signs have been showing up for weeks or even months. Pets are stoic by design, and many early changes are easy to miss unless you know what to watch for.

Why Awareness Changes Outcomes

Early detection genuinely changes the story. A small tumor is a different conversation than the same tumor caught late. A lymphoma caught at an early stage has treatment pathways that don't exist at a late stage. Removing a mast cell tumor with clean margins when it's small can be curative. Many internal changes begin long before any outward symptoms appear, which is why routine wellness exams and preventative lab work matter so much — they can catch things your eyes and hands can't.1

Awareness isn't paranoia. It's the simple practice of knowing your pet's normal and acting when something changes.

The Signs That Shouldn't Wait

The Animal Cancer Foundation, the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA), and veterinary oncologists broadly agree on the common warning signs. None of these on their own means cancer, but if any of them linger, worsen, or don't have an obvious explanation, it’s recommended to visit a vet sooner rather than later:2,3

  • Lumps and bumps, especially ones that change in size or shape — Not every lump is cancerous, but any new or changing growth deserves to be evaluated
  • Sores or ulcers that don't heal — Wounds that stay open past normal healing time (usually 10 to 14 days) can be more than they look
  • Change in appetite — A normally ravenous pet suddenly losing interest in food may have tumors making eating painful or triggering nausea
  • Unexplained weight loss — Losing weight without a change in diet is one of the most reliable early signals that something's off
  • Persistent bad breath — A strong odor that never improves can indicate a tumor (or diabetes, kidney, liver, or gum disease, all of which still warrant a vet visit)
  • Enlarged lymph nodes — Some lumps are actually swollen lymph nodes. Feel on either side of the jaw, in front of the shoulders, in the groin, and behind the knees
  • Vomiting or diarrhea that doesn't resolve — Frequent episodes signal illness and can cause dehydration if left untreated
  • Increased thirst or urination — A change in drinking or bathroom habits is often one of the earliest red flags for internal issues
  • Disinterest in usual activities — A pet who's lethargic, less playful, or no longer excited for walks and favorite things
  • Swollen abdomen — Call your vet immediately if your pet's belly begins to swell and they aren't pregnant; it can be caused by internal bleeding, tumors, parasites, or bloat
  • Persistent lameness, stiffness, or ongoing pain — If cancer invades the bones, walking or jumping becomes painful
  • Coughing or difficulty breathing — Persistent coughing or struggling to breathe needs urgent evaluation
  • Difficulty urinating or defecating — If your pet hasn't urinated in 24 hours, seems in pain, or strains to go, let your vet know right away. Trouble urinating can also signal a urinary blockage, which can be fatal without immediate treatment
  • Unexplained bleeding or discharge — From nose, mouth, ears, or any body opening, even if you only notice it once or twice
  • Any behavioral change that persists — If your pet seems "off," trust your instincts

Most pets will show one or more of these at some point in life without having cancer. Appetite dips happen. Dogs limp from running too hard. The point isn't to panic at the first symptom; it's to pay attention to the ones that linger, repeat, or come with other changes.

The Most Common Cancers to Know About

A few types of cancer show up most often in dogs and cats, and knowing them helps you connect what you're seeing on your pet to what might actually be going on inside. These are the ones worth having on your radar:4

  • Lymphoma — Affects the lymphatic system. Watch for swollen lymph nodes under the jaw, in front of the shoulders, or behind the knees.
  • Mast cell tumors — The most common skin cancer in dogs. They can look like almost any other lump: raised, flat, red, flesh-toned, hairy, or bald, and some change size from day to day. Any skin lump warrants a quick needle aspirate test.
  • Osteosarcoma — Bone cancer often occurs in large-breed dogs. Early signs include subtle limping, limb swelling, or reluctance to put weight on a leg.
  • Melanoma — A cancer of pigment-producing cells. It can show up as dark spots or lumps on the skin, inside the mouth, on the gums, or on the toes.
  • Mammary tumors — More common in intact female dogs and cats. Add regular belly checks for lumps along the chest and abdomen to your routine.

Build a Monthly Home Exam Habit

Veterinary experts routinely recommend a simple home practice: At least a few times a month, do a quiet five-minute hands-on check of your pet. You're not looking for anything specific — you're building a baseline. Over time, your hands will know what normal feels like, and anything new or changing will catch your attention sooner:

  • Run your hands slowly over the whole body, including the belly, armpits, around the ears, inside the thighs, and along the tail
  • Gently press along the lymph node areas under the jaw, in front of the shoulders, in the groin, and behind the knees
  • Look at the eyes, inside the mouth, and the teeth and gums; smell their breath
  • Check the paws, between the toes, and the nail beds
  • Watch for changes in stool, urine, and appetite over the following days
  • Note anything unusual in a quick log: size, location, and date

Cancer risk increases with age. Veterinary wellness guidelines recommend twice-yearly exams and bloodwork for senior pets, with ongoing monitoring for new lumps, appetite changes, or weight loss.5 Preventive lab testing in seniors often catches early changes months before visible symptoms appear. If something new shows up, don't wait for the next scheduled appointment; call your vet.

The Prevention Side

Not all cancers are preventable, and factors like genetics, age, or breed can play a role. However, a meaningful list of factors is within your influence, supported both by conventional veterinary guidance and the clinical experience of integrative and holistic vets:6,7

  • Diet — A fresh, species-appropriate, minimally processed diet gives the immune system the raw materials it needs. Reducing ultra-processed kibble, avoiding ingredients with industrial contaminants like heavy metals and bisphenol A (BPA), and skipping sugary or filler-heavy foods all matter.
  • Healthy weight — Obesity is linked to higher cancer risk in both dogs and cats. Keeping your pet at a lean body condition is one of the most under-discussed prevention tools available.
  • Environmental toxin reduction — Researchers have studied secondhand smoke, lawn chemicals, pesticides, household cleaners, and chemical-heavy flea and tick products for links to cancer in pets. Choose natural alternatives where possible — diatomaceous earth, cedarwood, essential-oil-based deterrents from reputable sources.
  • Sun protection for light-colored pets — Pets with white fur, pink noses, or thin coats are more vulnerable to UV-related skin cancers. Shade, timing walks outside peak sun hours, and pet-safe sunscreen on exposed areas all help.
  • Clean, filtered water — Standard tap water contains chlorine, chloramine, fluoride, and often traces of pharmaceuticals and heavy metals that increase lifetime exposure.
  • Movement and stress management — Daily walks and outdoor time support immune resilience. Chronic stress suppresses immune function in pets as much as in humans; a predictable routine, enrichment, and calm handling all help.
  • Integrative supplementation — Many integrative veterinarians use medicinal mushrooms (turkey tail, maitake, reishi), omega-3 fatty acids, antioxidants, and probiotic support as part of a long-term wellness plan. Talk with an integrative vet about what fits your specific pet.

If your pet is diagnosed with cancer, remain calm and work closely with your veterinary team. Diagnosis usually involves a physical exam, bloodwork, imaging like X-rays or ultrasound, and sampling the lump through a fine-needle aspirate or biopsy.

An integrative or holistic veterinary oncologist can be invaluable alongside conventional care, bringing nutrition, supplement protocols, acupuncture, and quality-of-life support into the plan. Pets with cancer today live longer, more comfortable lives than they did even a decade ago, and the combination of early detection and integrative care is a big part of why.

A Final Note

Spotting cancer before the signs get loud takes nothing more than knowing your pet, paying attention, and acting when something feels off. The monthly hands-on check. The twice-a-year vet visit for seniors. The willingness to call the vet about a lump instead of waiting. Clean food, filtered water, movement, and a lower-toxin home. None of this guarantees cancer prevention. But all of it stacks the odds — and dramatically improves what happens if a diagnosis does come.

This November, use Pet Cancer Awareness Month for what it's really worth: a prompt to look, touch, listen, and act. Your pet trusts you to notice. And the earlier you notice, the more you can do.

Sources and References

  • 1,5,7 Bluegrass Animal Hospital, November 2025
  • 2 Brigadoon Animal Hospital, November is Pet Cancer Awareness Month
  • 3,4,6 Pet Vet, November 6, 2024

item.title: The Trick Pet Companies Want You to Fall For
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Pet food companies are always researching new ways to control salmonella contamination, especially when it comes to kibble
  • A new potential additive being tested is 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutyric acid, or HMB, which is currently used in human dietary supplements for athletes and bodybuilders
  • One study concluded that HMB is effective at killing salmonella on dry pet food, and a manufacturer of HMB supplements has conducted pilot studies on the benefits of the chemical for working and racing dogs
  • If approved, it’s a given HMB will be marketed by pet food companies as a natural performance enhancer for canine athletes (with likely no mention that its also killing salmonella on the food)
  • Kibble sprayed with HMB is still kibble, which is biologically inappropriate nutrition for dogs and cats; it also comes with a long list of problematic ingredients that have the potential to cause degenerative disease in your pet

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published August 30, 2017.

Given the embarrassing number of processed pet food recalls over the years due to salmonella contamination, coupled with the FDA's zero-tolerance policy for salmonella in pet food and treats,1 as you might guess, one of the primary concerns of pet food manufacturers is the potential for salmonella contamination of their products, especially kibble.

As an aside, many people don't realize that salmonella infections from pet food are much more likely to occur in the humans handling it than the animals eating it, unless the pet is immunosuppressed or there's an unusually high level of contamination.

Dry pet food is heat-treated twice, once during pre-conditioning and again during extrusion, and the raw materials (such as meat meals) have been heated and processed extensively before being added to the kibble "batter." The very high temperatures used in these processing steps should kill the salmonella present in the food, however, recontamination can and does occur after the food is extruded — possibly inside the conveying system or from airborne dust in air-handling systems.

There are a number of tactics pet food producers use to control salmonella contamination, including vendor inspections, hazard analysis and critical control point plans and hold-and-release programs. Potential additives, some of them quite bizarre, are also routinely investigated for their ability to control salmonella.

Study Investigates Bodybuilding Supplement for Use in Salmonella Control

One such substance being studied is 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutyric acid (HMB, not to be confused with 3-hydroxybutyric acid). HMB is a breakdown product of the amino acid leucine. Small amounts of HMB are present in certain foods, including alfalfa, asparagus, avocados, cauliflower, grapefruit, catfish and milk.2 HMB is also naturally synthesized in the human body. It's produced by the liver and muscles, and is thought to be involved in muscle protein synthesis.3

HMB is sold as a dietary supplement to (human) athletes and exercisers who want to add muscle mass and reduce recovery times. It's also found in certain medical foods designed to provide nutritional support to people with diseases that cause muscle wasting, as well as to promote wound healing after surgery or injury.

If you're wondering how a bodybuilding supplement has anything to do with controlling salmonella on dry pet food, welcome to the club. For reasons known only to them, recently a manufacturer of HMB supplements and scientists at Kansas State University conducted a study on the ability of the chemical to prevent recontamination by salmonella after the pet food extrusion process.4

Can Spraying HMB on Kibble Help Control Salmonella Contamination?

The researchers ran three trials using five different concentrations of two forms of HMB sprayed onto kibble post-extrusion. After spraying the HMB, they injected the dry food with a strain of salmonella bacteria. The control kibble sample did not get treated with HMB, but did get exposed to the salmonella.

At specific intervals over the next two weeks, the researchers measured the kibble for the presence of bacteria, and observed that the HMB reduced salmonella growth compared to the control sample. At the end of the two weeks, the HMB had eliminated detectable salmonella contamination on the treated samples. Study author John Fuller, Ph.D., told PetfoodIndustry.com:

"As with any scientific hypothesis, it generally takes repeated studies to have widely accepted support for the hypothesis. We are confident in the data we have generated as this was generated in two independent laboratory settings. Thus, this could provide the basis for commercial use; however, these results should be repeated in an actual commercial setting."5

HMB Provides yet Another Marketing Opportunity for Pet Food Companies

How fortunate is it for processed pet food manufacturers that a chemical that appears to kill salmonella in finished product kibble also just happens to be an athletic performance supplement? According to PetfoodIndustry.com:

"HMB can be found on the shelves of dietary supplement stores, where it is marketed as a means to build lean muscle and speed healing after hard weightlifting sessions. Also, physiologists and biologists have found empirical evidence to back up those marketing claims."

Study co-author Fuller, who works for an HMB supplement manufacturer, believes the chemical may provide similar benefits for working and athletic dogs.

"The intended use would be as an anti-microbial when added to or coated on the food," says Fuller, "but yes it could have a physiological effect as well similar to the effect seen in humans."

Studies of HMB in humans and horses show the substance does help with recovery from strenuous exercise, and helps athletes of both species "train and work harder." There are no published studies involving dogs, but Fuller's company has done some pilot studies that indicate "a distinct benefit for racing and working dogs."

Needless to say, when and if HMB is approved for use in pet food, its benefit as a salmonella killer won't be mentioned on product advertising, but you can bet its potential to improve the condition, performance and recovery of working and athletic dogs will be.

Lipstick on a Pig

The good news is pet food companies are actively searching for ways to reduce exposure to salmonella bacteria in their products. And as chemical pet food additives go, 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutyric acid appears to be relatively benign. The bad news? Adding a substance like HMB to dry pet food is a little like putting lipstick on a pig (no offense to pigs, since they're actually quite adorable). The pig may look more attractive, but it's still a pig.

Salmonella-free kibble is still kibble. Aside from poor-quality meats, byproducts and synthetic vitamins and minerals, most commercial dry pet foods are built around high glycemic, genetically engineered (GE) corn, wheat, rice or potato — grains and starches that have no place in your pet's diet and create metabolically stressful insulin, glucagon and cortisol spikes throughout the day.

In fact, many grain-free dry foods have a higher glycemic index than pet foods containing grain due to the excessive amounts of potatoes, peas, lentils or tapioca included in the formulas.

Carbs also break down into sugar, which fuels degenerative conditions such as diabetes, obesity and cancer. In the last 50 years we've learned the hard way that feeding biologically inappropriate, low-fat, high-carb diets do not create health in pets. In fact, chronic inflammatory and degenerative diseases have reached epidemic levels, all related to diet and lifestyle.

Further, low-quality proteins and fats (not fit for human consumption), when processed at high temperatures, create cancerous byproducts like heterocyclic amines.

The low moisture content of dry food is also problematic, especially for cats. Dry cat food provides only about one-tenth the amount of moisture cats receive from prey animals, living foods and even commercial canned diets, which puts significant stress on their kidneys and bladder.

Dogs also tend to become excessively thirsty when fed kibble exclusively. The carb-heavy nature of dry food, along with the tendency of pet parents to overfeed, is also a significant factor in rising rates of pet obesity. Most dogs and cats will thrive when given fresh, whole foods that mimic their ancestral diet, but unfortunately, many should make do with entirely processed, largely inferior alternatives. Your pet may have adapted to this diet, but it's a recipe for chronic disease.

The Recommendation

As mentioned earlier, the danger of salmonella poisoning from pet food is primarily a risk to the humans serving the food, not the animals eating it. Healthy pets are able to handle a much higher bacterial load than their owners. If you feed your pet kibble (which again, is not recommended), the following simple handling precautions should keep you and your family safe from contamination:

  • Wash your hands thoroughly after handling any pet food or treats.
  • Don't allow very young children, elderly people or those who are immunocompromised to handle pet food or treats.
  • Keep all pet foods and treats away from your family's food.
  • Do not prepare pet foods in the same area or with the same equipment/utensils you use to prepare human foods.
  • Do not allow pets on countertops or other areas where human food is prepared.
  • Feeding pets in the kitchen has been identified as a source of infection. If you can arrange to feed your pet in an area other than your kitchen, consider doing so. Alternatively, feed your pet as far away from human food preparation areas as possible.

Feeding a commercial pet food with special additives designed to control salmonella isn't recommended. Wholesome, natural diets are preferred for pets (and people).

Sources and References

  • 1 FDA.gov (Archived)
  • 2 Wikipedia, β-Hydroxy β-methylbutyric acid
  • 3 Living Naturally
  • 4 Journal of Food Protection. 2017 Jul;80(7):1080-1084
  • 5 PetfoodIndustry.com, July 5, 2017

HMB is sold as a dietary supplement to (human) athletes and exercisers who want to add muscle mass and reduce recovery times. It's also found in certain medical foods designed to provide nutritional support to people with diseases that cause muscle wasting, as well as to promote wound healing after surgery or injury.

If you're wondering how a bodybuilding supplement has anything to do with controlling salmonella on dry pet food, welcome to the club. For reasons known only to them, recently a manufacturer of HMB supplements and scientists at Kansas State University conducted a study on the ability of the chemical to prevent recontamination by salmonella after the pet food extrusion process.4

Can Spraying HMB on Kibble Help Control Salmonella Contamination?

The researchers ran three trials using five different concentrations of two forms of HMB sprayed onto kibble post-extrusion. After spraying the HMB, they injected the dry food with a strain of salmonella bacteria. The control kibble sample did not get treated with HMB, but did get exposed to the salmonella.

At specific intervals over the next two weeks, the researchers measured the kibble for the presence of bacteria, and observed that the HMB reduced salmonella growth compared to the control sample. At the end of the two weeks, the HMB had eliminated detectable salmonella contamination on the treated samples. Study author John Fuller, Ph.D., told PetfoodIndustry.com:

"As with any scientific hypothesis, it generally takes repeated studies to have widely accepted support for the hypothesis. We are confident in the data we have generated as this was generated in two independent laboratory settings. Thus, this could provide the basis for commercial use; however, these results should be repeated in an actual commercial setting."5

HMB Provides yet Another Marketing Opportunity for Pet Food Companies

How fortunate is it for processed pet food manufacturers that a chemical that appears to kill salmonella in finished product kibble also just happens to be an athletic performance supplement? According to PetfoodIndustry.com:

"HMB can be found on the shelves of dietary supplement stores, where it is marketed as a means to build lean muscle and speed healing after hard weightlifting sessions. Also, physiologists and biologists have found empirical evidence to back up those marketing claims."

Study co-author Fuller, who works for an HMB supplement manufacturer, believes the chemical may provide similar benefits for working and athletic dogs.

"The intended use would be as an anti-microbial when added to or coated on the food," says Fuller, "but yes it could have a physiological effect as well similar to the effect seen in humans."

Studies of HMB in humans and horses show the substance does help with recovery from strenuous exercise, and helps athletes of both species "train and work harder." There are no published studies involving dogs, but Fuller's company has done some pilot studies that indicate "a distinct benefit for racing and working dogs."

Needless to say, when and if HMB is approved for use in pet food, its benefit as a salmonella killer won't be mentioned on product advertising, but you can bet its potential to improve the condition, performance and recovery of working and athletic dogs will be.

Lipstick on a Pig

The good news is pet food companies are actively searching for ways to reduce exposure to salmonella bacteria in their products. And as chemical pet food additives go, 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutyric acid appears to be relatively benign. The bad news? Adding a substance like HMB to dry pet food is a little like putting lipstick on a pig (no offense to pigs, since they're actually quite adorable). The pig may look more attractive, but it's still a pig.

Salmonella-free kibble is still kibble. Aside from poor-quality meats, byproducts and synthetic vitamins and minerals, most commercial dry pet foods are built around high glycemic, genetically engineered (GE) corn, wheat, rice or potato — grains and starches that have no place in your pet's diet and create metabolically stressful insulin, glucagon and cortisol spikes throughout the day.

In fact, many grain-free dry foods have a higher glycemic index than pet foods containing grain due to the excessive amounts of potatoes, peas, lentils or tapioca included in the formulas.

Carbs also break down into sugar, which fuels degenerative conditions such as diabetes, obesity and cancer. In the last 50 years we've learned the hard way that feeding biologically inappropriate, low-fat, high-carb diets do not create health in pets. In fact, chronic inflammatory and degenerative diseases have reached epidemic levels, all related to diet and lifestyle.

Further, low-quality proteins and fats (not fit for human consumption), when processed at high temperatures, create cancerous byproducts like heterocyclic amines.

The low moisture content of dry food is also problematic, especially for cats. Dry cat food provides only about one-tenth the amount of moisture cats receive from prey animals, living foods and even commercial canned diets, which puts significant stress on their kidneys and bladder.

Dogs also tend to become excessively thirsty when fed kibble exclusively. The carb-heavy nature of dry food, along with the tendency of pet parents to overfeed, is also a significant factor in rising rates of pet obesity. Most dogs and cats will thrive when given fresh, whole foods that mimic their ancestral diet, but unfortunately, many should make do with entirely processed, largely inferior alternatives. Your pet may have adapted to this diet, but it's a recipe for chronic disease.

The Recommendation

As mentioned earlier, the danger of salmonella poisoning from pet food is primarily a risk to the humans serving the food, not the animals eating it. Healthy pets are able to handle a much higher bacterial load than their owners. If you feed your pet kibble (which again, is not recommended), the following simple handling precautions should keep you and your family safe from contamination:

  • Wash your hands thoroughly after handling any pet food or treats.
  • Don't allow very young children, elderly people or those who are immunocompromised to handle pet food or treats.
  • Keep all pet foods and treats away from your family's food.
  • Do not prepare pet foods in the same area or with the same equipment/utensils you use to prepare human foods.
  • Do not allow pets on countertops or other areas where human food is prepared.
  • Feeding pets in the kitchen has been identified as a source of infection. If you can arrange to feed your pet in an area other than your kitchen, consider doing so. Alternatively, feed your pet as far away from human food preparation areas as possible.

Feeding a commercial pet food with special additives designed to control salmonella isn't recommended. Wholesome, natural diets are preferred for pets (and people).

item.title: One Little Kitchen Scrap Can Cause Big Trouble
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Around 105 billion pounds of onions are grown each year, and the average annual consumption per person is 13.67 pounds
  • According to research, as little as 5 grams of onions per kilogram of body weight in cats, or 15 to 30 grams per kilogram in dogs, may create drastic hematologic changes
  • Onions can cause damage to red blood cells in animals once consumed
  • If you keep allium vegetables in your kitchen, get a pet-proof container to store them in
  • If you believe your pet has consumed onions, contact your veterinarian immediately

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published January 24, 2022.

Onions are one of the most commonly used vegetables around the world. According to the National Onion Association, around 105 billion pounds of onions are grown each year, and the average annual consumption per person is 13.67 pounds.1

It’s highly probable that from the billions of pounds of onions cultivated annually, some small scraps will eventually be consumed by household pets. However, onions are one of the vegetables that you should avoid feeding to your pet, as they may pose health risks.

Did You Know?

The origin of the onion isn’t clear, but historians generally agree that it came from central Asia. Prehistoric humans most likely consumed onions long before agriculture came into existence.2

The Allium Plant Family Isn’t Generally Recommended for Pets

Members of the allium plant family have various organosulfur compounds and polyphenols that hold tremendous potential for optimal well-being in humans.3 However, these same compounds can make your beloved pet sick.

According to a study published in Interdisciplinary Toxicology, the compounds inherent in onions may cause damage to a pet’s red blood cells and even cause hemolytic anemia. Furthermore, researchers noted that not only cats and dogs are affected, but other animals as well, such as cattle and horses.4 The actual mechanism of action isn’t fully understood, but this is what the researchers observed:5

“The toxic components in all type of onions, garlic, leeks, shallots, and other plants of the Allium family, are sulfoxides and aliphatic sulfides, specifically allyl and propyl di-, tri-, and tetrasulfides. Onions contain also the relatively rare amino acids S-meth and S-prop (en)ylcysteine sulfoxides (SMCO).
It is widely agreed that n-propyl disulphide is the principal toxin that reduces the activity of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in red blood cells; thereby interfering with regeneration of reduced glutathione needed to prevent oxidative denaturation of haemoglobin. Denaturated haemoglobin, when developed, precipitates on the surface of red blood cells (named Heinz bodies) and triggers intra- and extravascular haemolysis. The haemolytic effect of sodium n-propylthiosulphate, which had been isolated from boiled onions, was studied in dogs by Yamato et al. (19986).”

That being said, in the case of garlic very large quantities are needed to be dangerous — much more than you would typically feed to your dog. Dogs can healthfully consume 1/4 teaspoon of freshly chopped garlic per 15 pounds of body weight and reap substantial health benefits, just don't overdo it.

Which Country Grows the Most Onions?

China is the world’s top producer of onions, producing over 20,507,759 tons in 2018. India trails closely with 13,372,100 tons. Third place belongs to the U.S., with 3,320,870 tons.7

What Are the Signs of Allium Poisoning in Your Pet?

“Consumption of even a small amount of onions may produce side effects in animals.”

According to research, as little as 5 grams of onions per kilogram of body weight in cats, or 15 to 30 grams per kilogram in dogs, may create drastic hematologic changes.8 Health problems may appear within a day of consumption (if eaten in large amounts) or several days later. If you think your pet has consumed onions, here are telltale symptoms you need to watch out for:9

  • Vomiting
  • Diarrhea
  • Abdominal pain
  • Smell of onion in breath
  • Loss of appetite
  • Depression
  • Dehydration

If the red blood cells have already been damaged, these symptoms may appear:10

  • Pale mucous membranes
  • Rapid respiratory rate
  • Rapid heart rate
  • Difficulty breathing
  • Lethargy
  • Dark-colored urine (reddish or brown)
  • Jaundice
  • Weakness
  • Depression
  • Sensitivity to cold

Onion Trivia

Onions are notorious for making people cry in the kitchen. This is because of their defense mechanism, which is a chemical known as lachrymatory factor. When the flesh is crushed or sliced, the chemical is released and irritates the eyes to ward off predators.11

What to Do if Your Pet Accidentally Ate Onions

If your pet just ate onions (including leeks and chives), contact your veterinarian immediately. Any food or dish that contains onion, even in small amounts, may harm your pet.12

There is no specific cure for allium toxicity among pets. Instead, treatment focuses on supporting the pet’s body for optimal recovery. However, there are approaches that may require medical intervention. Examples include gastrointestinal decontamination, intravenous therapy and administration of vitamins C and E. In more severe cases, blood transfusion and supplemental oxygen therapy may be required.13 Your veterinarian will decide which strategy is the best to facilitate a full recovery for your pet.

For Your Pet’s Safety, Don’t Leave Onions Out in the Open

Based on the published evidence, it’s clear that you shouldn’t feed onions — or any food that contains alliums — to your dog or cat. If you keep allium vegetables in your kitchen, get a pet-proof container to store them in. Knowing that onions (and other dangerous foods) are safely stored away from your pet will give you peace of mind whenever your pet decides to wander into the kitchen.

Sources and References

  • 1 National Onion Association, Consumption
  • 2 National Onion Association, Onion History
  • 3 Antioxidants (Basel). 2020 Sep; 19(9): 888, Abstract
  • 4,5,8,12 Interdiscip Toxicol. 2009 Sep 28;2(3):169–176
  • 6 Vet Rec. 1998;142(9):216–219
  • 7 Current Anthropology, 3(2), June 2018, Table 3
  • 9,10 The Journal of Venomous Animals and Toxins including Tropical Diseases, Volume 17, Issue 1, Pages 4-11, Clinical Signs
  • 11 The New York Times, September 5, 2017
  • 13 The Journal of Venomous Animals and Toxins including Tropical Diseases, volume 17, issue 1, Pages 4-11, Treatment

item.title: Giving Your Dog Plenty of This Might Help Prevent Lymphoma
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • A study of golden retrievers with T-zone lymphoma suggests that dogs eating diets rich in omega-3 essential fatty acids may be less likely to develop the disease
  • Omega-3s are simply the superstars of essential fatty acids in terms of the significant health benefits they offer pets
  • Studies show omega-3s are beneficial for the healthy development of puppies and for dogs with anxiety, arthritis, heart disease, chronic kidney disease and itchy, inflamed skin
  • The best sources of omega-3s are fish body oils
  • Fish body oils without vitamin D are preferred for pets, since too much vitamin A and D from fish liver oils can cause toxicosis

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published July 3, 2019.

Canine T-zone lymphoma (TZL) is a slowly progressive form of cancer most often seen in older dogs, comprising about 12% of canine lymphoma cases. This type of lymphoma is far more prevalent in golden retrievers than any other breed, accounting for 40% of all cases.1

A team of researchers at Colorado State University's (CSU) College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences conducted a study to evaluate associations of genetics, environment, lifestyle and health history of T-zone lymphoma in Goldens. Their results were published in the Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine.2

Study — Omega-3 Fatty Acids May Provide Protection Against T-Zone Lymphoma in Dogs

The dogs were recruited from Morris Animal Foundation's Canine Lifetime Health Project Registry. Many of the dogs were entered into the registry to be enrolled in the foundation's Golden Retriever Lifetime Study but were too old to participate. For the study, the researchers analyzed detailed health history questionnaires and blood or biological samples from more than 350 Goldens that were split into a group of dogs with TZL, and a control group of healthy dogs who were at least 9 years old.

The health history questionnaires covered topics such as the dogs' living situation, vaccination history and potential exposure to toxins. The researchers used blood samples to try to locate areas in the dogs' chromosomes associated with having or not having the disease. The study results indicate that dogs receiving omega-3 fatty acid supplements may be less likely to develop T-zone lymphoma. (Interestingly, dogs with hypothyroidism are also at decreased risk.)

"Although controlled prospective studies would be necessary to firmly establish protection by omega-3 fatty acids, our observations raise the possibility of a simple intervention that may help reduce the frequency of this disease," said Dr. Anne Avery, associate professor, department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pathology at Colorado State University.
"We were also a little surprised to discover that defective genes that lead to another, seemingly unrelated disorder — hypothyroidism — are more common in dogs that do not develop T-zone lymphoma."3

While the study focused on Goldens, Dr. Avery believes the underlying causes of TZL are shared across breeds. These findings support what Dr. Anna Hielm-Björkman and her Helsinki Vet School DogRisk project also discovered — dogs, regardless of breed that were supplemented with fish oil had less cancer than unsupplemented dogs.

Omega-3s — the Superstars of Essential Fatty Acids

One of the fastest growing categories of pet supplements is fish oil aka fish body oil, a rich source of essential fatty acids (EFAs), more commonly known as omega-6 and omega-3 fats. While dogs (and cats) need a balance of both for good health, omega-3s are the superstars in terms of the significant health benefits they offer.

Omega-3 fatty acids include alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), which play a role in your pet's overall health in many ways, including:

  • Alleviating the harmful effects of allergies and other conditions that result from an over-reactive immune system response
  • Slowing the growth of common yeast infections
  • Regulating blood-clotting activity
  • Aiding proper development of the retina and visual cortex
  • Slowing the development and spread of certain types of cancer

Along with these benefits, multiple clinical studies show that omega-3s are helpful in the prevention and treatment of several conditions involving the cardiovascular system, cognitive function, neurological health, inflammatory skin disease, kidney disease and osteoarthritis.

DHA Is Beneficial for Puppies

A study published in 2012 indicates that feeding newly weaned puppies foods high in DHA has wide-ranging health benefits.4 The goal of the study was to evaluate the effect of food with added DHA from fish oil on the cognitive, memory, psychomotor, immunologic, retinal function and other developmental measures in 48 healthy, newly weaned 8-week-old Beagle puppies.

The researchers observed that the puppies fed diets containing the highest levels of DHA had significantly better results than the other groups in reversal learning tasks, visual contrast discrimination and early psychomotor performance. They also had significantly higher rabies antibody titers one and two weeks after vaccination, and an improved ability to see in low-light or dark conditions.

EPA Calms Anxious Dogs

Dogs suffering with anxiety may benefit from supplementation with a high-quality source of omega-3 fats, due to their ability to modulate neurotransmitters and neuroplasticity in the brain. In 2008, researchers compared the omega-3 fat EPA against the antidepressant drug fluoxetine (Prozac) and discovered EPA was just as effective as the drug in relieving symptoms of depression in humans, and the same may be true for dogs.5

Subsequent research involving 24 dogs found increased intake of omega-3 fats had a calming effect on anxious dogs and led to improvements in behavior.6

EPA and DHA Improve Symptoms in Arthritic Dogs

A 2013 Canadian study indicates that omega-3s are beneficial for dogs with naturally occurring osteoarthritis.7 The dogs were fed a diet containing high levels of omega-3 fatty acids from fish and showed significant improvement in locomotor disability and performance of daily activities.

Omega-3s Improve Cardiac Function in Dogs with Heart Disease

In a 1998 study of dogs with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), omega-3 supplementation reduced production of inflammatory cytokines (interleukin-1 and prostaglandin E2), and also reduced muscle loss compared with a placebo.8 The decreased production of inflammatory cytokines is also thought to improve appetites in animals with heart failure.

In a retrospective study of 108 dogs with DCM or chronic valvular disease, results showed improved survival rates with omega-3 fatty acid supplementation.9 In addition to improved heart function (including reduced heart rate and blood pressure), omega-3 supplementation also reduced inflammation and improved the dogs' appetite and maintenance of lean body mass.

Omega-3s Improve Chronic Kidney Disease Survival Times

In a study of dogs with chronic kidney disease (CKD), researchers demonstrated that supplementation with omega-6 fatty acids accelerates the decline of kidney function, while omega-3s do the opposite.10

EPA Significantly Improves Itchy, Inflamed Skin

In a 1994 study of 16 dogs given omega-3 fatty acids that included high levels of EPA showed improvement in itchiness, self-trauma, coat character and hair loss compared with administration of ALA alone.11 The dogs in the study had symptoms of idiopathic pruritus (unexplained itchy skin), confirmed atopy (inflamed skin due to allergies) and/or flea allergy.

A 2014 study evaluated a spot-on formulation of essential fatty acids and essential oils on 48 dogs with canine atopic dermatitis. The results showed that individual improvements in lesion and itchiness scores were significantly higher for dogs that received the EFAs and essential oils versus the control group, and more of those dogs also showed a 50% or greater improvement in itchiness.12

The Best Sources of Omega-3 Fatty Acids

Processed pet food is manufactured at very high temperatures, and since omega-3 fatty acids are sensitive to heat and light, they are inert by the time they are packaged. Even if you feed your pet homemade raw meals, if you're not following a balanced recipe that calls for extra essential fatty acids (omega-3s from seafood), your dog's diet is probably unbalanced for fatty acids.

Not only are omega-3s important, so is the dietary ratio of omega-3s to omega-6s. Because the average pet diet is heavy in omega-6s, supplementing with additional omega-6s in the form of corn, olive, safflower or even flax oil (which contains some vegetable sources of omega-3s, but also omega-6s) can create an imbalance that can lead to health problems.

Krill oil is the recommended supplement to ensure your pet is getting enough omega-3 fats in his diet. Dogs can’t efficiently convert plant sources of omega-3 fatty acids (from flaxseed oil, for example) into appropriate amounts of DHA and EPA, so the best option is to provide one in its already bioavailable form from marine oils.

As noted, omega-3s are very sensitive to oxygen and can become rancid quickly, so oils either dispensed from an airless pump or in capsules that can be cut and squeezed onto food just prior to feeding are preferred. With "pour on" oils there is a far greater risk of oxidation over time, so if you do purchase a bottle, make sure to refrigerate it after opening and try to use it up within 30 days.

Try to ensure your fish oil is sustainably harvested, or MSC-approved, and comes from nontoxic fish (the smaller the better, hence the recommendation of krill oil). Many people afraid to feed fish from the ocean find comfort in the third party-validated, toxin-free marine oils available in the market. Unlike fish, fish oils can be tested for purity and potency. If you have concerns about the quality of your fish oil, ask the manufacturer to provide you with third party testing results that demonstrates the product is toxin-free.

Cod liver oil and other fish liver oils, while rich in omega-3 fatty acids, are also very high in vitamins A and D. Since dogs eating commercial pet foods are already getting adequate amounts of these fat-soluble vitamins, too much can result in toxicosis or abnormal calcium and phosphorus levels that can cause mineralization and calcification of vital tissue and organs, as well as urinary stones. That's why fish body oils without vitamin D are preferred for pets.

It's important to seek the advice of an integrative veterinarian to determine how to best supplement your dog's diet with the fatty acids he needs for good health and to treat any specific health conditions he may have.

The health history questionnaires covered topics such as the dogs' living situation, vaccination history and potential exposure to toxins. The researchers used blood samples to try to locate areas in the dogs' chromosomes associated with having or not having the disease. The study results indicate that dogs receiving omega-3 fatty acid supplements may be less likely to develop T-zone lymphoma. (Interestingly, dogs with hypothyroidism are also at decreased risk.)

"Although controlled prospective studies would be necessary to firmly establish protection by omega-3 fatty acids, our observations raise the possibility of a simple intervention that may help reduce the frequency of this disease," said Dr. Anne Avery, associate professor, department of Microbiology, Immunology and Pathology at Colorado State University.
"We were also a little surprised to discover that defective genes that lead to another, seemingly unrelated disorder — hypothyroidism — are more common in dogs that do not develop T-zone lymphoma."3

While the study focused on Goldens, Dr. Avery believes the underlying causes of TZL are shared across breeds. These findings support what Dr. Anna Hielm-Björkman and her Helsinki Vet School DogRisk project also discovered — dogs, regardless of breed that were supplemented with fish oil had less cancer than unsupplemented dogs.

One of the fastest growing categories of pet supplements is fish oil aka fish body oil, a rich source of essential fatty acids (EFAs), more commonly known as omega-6 and omega-3 fats. While dogs (and cats) need a balance of both for good health, omega-3s are the superstars in terms of the significant health benefits they offer.

Omega-3 fatty acids include alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), which play a role in your pet's overall health in many ways, including:

  • Alleviating the harmful effects of allergies and other conditions that result from an over-reactive immune system response
  • Slowing the growth of common yeast infections
  • Regulating blood-clotting activity
  • Aiding proper development of the retina and visual cortex
  • Slowing the development and spread of certain types of cancer

Along with these benefits, multiple clinical studies show that omega-3s are helpful in the prevention and treatment of several conditions involving the cardiovascular system, cognitive function, neurological health, inflammatory skin disease, kidney disease and osteoarthritis.

DHA Is Beneficial for Puppies

A study published in 2012 indicates that feeding newly weaned puppies foods high in DHA has wide-ranging health benefits.4 The goal of the study was to evaluate the effect of food with added DHA from fish oil on the cognitive, memory, psychomotor, immunologic, retinal function and other developmental measures in 48 healthy, newly weaned 8-week-old Beagle puppies.

In a 1994 study of 16 dogs given omega-3 fatty acids that included high levels of EPA showed improvement in itchiness, self-trauma, coat character and hair loss compared with administration of ALA alone.11 The dogs in the study had symptoms of idiopathic pruritus (unexplained itchy skin), confirmed atopy (inflamed skin due to allergies) and/or flea allergy.

If you have concerns about the quality of your fish oil, ask the manufacturer to provide you with third party testing results that demonstrates the product is toxin-free.

item.title: What Are Those Funny Little Bumps Trying to Tell You?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Dog warts are benign growths that can be caused by canine papillomavirus (CPV), with 24 different types now identified — most affecting either the skin or the mouth, and most resolving on their own without any medical intervention
  • Puppies and adolescent dogs are most commonly affected because their immune systems are still learning to recognize new viruses, while senior dogs may develop slower-growing skin warts as immune function naturally declines with age and with hormone changes
  • The classic papilloma-type dog wart has a rough cauliflower texture, appears in clusters or singly around the mouth, eyes, face, paws, or ears, and usually resolves within four to eight weeks for oral warts and about three months for skin warts
  • Canine papillomavirus is species-specific — dogs cannot pass it to cats, other pets, or humans, and the virus typically enters through tiny skin breaks or moist areas like the mouth
  • Integrative and holistic veterinarians focus on supporting the immune system with real-food diets, gut health, immune-supportive nutrients, medicinal mushrooms, stress reduction, and homeopathic remedies rather than jumping to invasive interventions

You are scratching your dog's chin one afternoon and your fingers find something new — a small, rough bump that was not there last week. It looks a little like a tiny cauliflower, and it does not seem to bother them. You check for more, and see another one on their lip, and a third on their paw — so what are these unusual growths?

There is a good chance you are looking at a viral wart. And while any new lump on your dog deserves attention, the good news is that most of these particular bumps are far more of a cosmetic issue than a medical crisis. They are actually your dog's immune system sending a signal — and once you understand what they are, they become much less alarming.

What These Bumps Actually Are

Viral dog warts are benign growths caused by canine papillomavirus (CPV). Researchers have now identified 24 different types of canine papillomavirus, most of which affect either the skin or the mouth. Cats have their own version, feline papillomavirus, with six types identified so far. Both species carry papillomaviruses commonly, though visible warts are far more frequent in dogs than cats.1

The virus works by entering skin cells through tiny breaks — a small cut from rough play, a scratch from grass, a naturally moist area like the mouth — and hijacking normal cell growth to create the characteristic bumpy texture we recognize as a wart. The immune system then gradually recognizes the invader and mounts a response, which is what eventually clears the wart.2

Who Gets Them and Why

Cutaneous warts are actually the second most frequent skin tumor in dogs under one year of age. Puppies and adolescent dogs are the classic patients because their immune systems are still learning to recognize new viruses, and their tendency to mouth and chew everything in sight gives the virus plenty of entry points. Oral warts in particular tend to show up in dogs under about 18 months.3

Older dogs — usually over about seven years — also develop warts, though a different flavor of them. These warts tend to show up on the body and tend to not be papillomavirus related; they are generally sebaceous adenomas, benign growths stemming out of the sebaceous gland. Their warts tend to be slower-growing skin warts rather than the classic oral clusters, and they show up as pet's experience age-related changes in skin barrier health, hormone balance, and immune function.

Certain breeds may be more susceptible to papillomavirus based on various meta-analyses of case reports and geographic studies: Pugs and Miniature Schnauzers are known to be predisposed to the viral cutaneous plaque form of papillomavirus, and case reports of this in Vizslas have emerged. Other breeds including again Miniature Schnauzers and Labrador retrievers have been reported to be predisposed to the papillomatous form of the disease.

Anything that suppresses immune function — chronic stress, poor diet, illness, being on immunosuppressive medication — makes any dog more vulnerable regardless of breed. And in females, hormonal changes such as coming into heat for the first time can also lower immune resilience temporarily.4

What They Look Like

The classic dog wart has a rough, cauliflower-like texture that feels firm to the touch. They can appear as single growths or in clusters, and they range from the size of a grain of rice to the size of a small grape. Some look feathery or scaly, and the color usually matches your dog's skin — flesh-toned, pink, or slightly darker. Common places to find them include:

  • Mouth, lips, and gums (especially in puppies)
  • Around the eyes and eyelids
  • On the face and muzzle
  • Ears and ear flaps
  • Between the toes and on paw pads
  • Occasionally on the genital area

Fresh warts often appear pink or flesh-colored. Older ones may darken or develop a crusty surface as the immune system begins fighting back. Warts on the mouth deserve a little extra attention since they can sometimes interfere with eating in severe cases, but this is uncommon.5

How They Spread

The virus spreads through direct contact — saliva, shared toys, food and water bowls, bedding — with an infected dog or with a dog who is carrying the virus without symptoms. Inoculation of the virus requires a microtear or injury in the skin surface for the virus to transfer. The incubation period is typically four to six weeks, which means a wart you are spotting today came from an exposure over a month ago. That timeline is actually reassuring: the situation is not an immediate emergency, and your dog's immune system has already been working on it for weeks.

The species boundary is important to know. Canine papillomavirus affects only dogs. Your cats, your family members, and other pets in the household are not at risk of catching it from your dog. Feline papillomavirus works the same way — cats cannot give it to dogs, and neither species passes it to humans.6,7

The Reassuring Part

Most canine cutaneous warts regress spontaneously within about three months, and most oral warts resolve within four to eight weeks. From an integrative and holistic veterinary perspective, the appearance of warts is often best understood as a sign that your dog's immune system is actively engaging with and building resistance to the virus — much the way children develop resistance to common viruses as they grow. Progression from a benign wart to something more serious like a squamous cell carcinoma is extremely rare, and typically only happens in dogs with significant immune suppression.8,9

Warts may actually appear to worsen slightly before improvement begins — this represents immune activation, not treatment failure. During the first couple of weeks you may see little visible change. Significant improvement usually shows up during weeks 5 through 7, with complete resolution by around week 8 in most straightforward cases.

Supporting Your Dog's Immune Response

Since a strong immune system is what actually clears the virus, the most useful thing you can do is support that system. Integrative and holistic veterinarians commonly focus on:10

  • Species-appropriate diet — High-quality, minimally processed, real-food feeding — with plenty of clean protein, healthy fats, and appropriate carbohydrates — provides the raw materials your dog's immune system uses to build defenses. Fresh food matters more than most pet parents realize when it comes to immune resilience.
  • Gut health support — A significant portion of the immune system lives in the gut. A good-quality probiotic and prebiotic combination, along with digestive enzymes if needed, can help keep the immune foundation strong.
  • Immune-supportive nutrients — Vitamin C, vitamin D at appropriate levels, EPA and DHA, and chlorella are all commonly used in holistic protocols. A methyl donor like DMG (dimethylglycine) or SAMe is sometimes added. Talk to an integrative vet about supplements and doses appropriate for your specific dog.
  • Medicinal mushrooms — Extracts like maitake D-fraction, reishi, and turkey tail are widely used to support immune modulation in dogs. Look for veterinary-grade formulations rather than human supplements.
  • Stress reduction — Emotional, physical, and environmental stressors all suppress immune function. A calm household routine, plenty of rest, appropriate exercise, and time outdoors all matter. Even minor adjustments — reducing loud noises during recovery, keeping feeding schedules predictable — can help.
  • Homeopathic support — Many holistic veterinarians reach for constitutional homeopathic remedies matched to the specific dog's overall symptom picture, rather than a generic wart remedy. Working with a veterinary homeopath can produce genuinely impressive results for some dogs.

Home Care While You Wait

A few practical things can help while the immune system does its work. None of them will make the warts vanish overnight, but they do prevent the small problems that can turn a straightforward viral wart into a bigger issue:

  • Discourage licking, chewing, or scratching at wart sites — the trauma can introduce bacteria and slow healing
  • Do a gentle daily check for changes in size, color, or new growths
  • Clean any discharge around a wart site gently with warm water
  • Consider weekly photos in similar lighting to track real progress objectively
  • Separate food and water bowls, toys, and bedding from other dogs in the household during the active wart phase
  • Continue normal exercise, play, and socialization — strict isolation is not necessary or helpful
  • If your dog is a persistent licker, a soft recovery collar worn briefly during unsupervised time prevents wart trauma without adding stress

When to Call the Vet

Most warts do not need medical intervention. But there are situations that warrant a professional look, such as:

  • A bump that is smooth and dome-shaped, unusually hard or soft, or growing rapidly over days rather than weeks
  • Signs of pain when the area is touched
  • Bleeding, discharge, warmth, or swelling around the growth
  • Warts that interfere with eating, drinking, or breathing
  • Warts that persist well beyond the typical eight-to-twelve-week window without any sign of improvement
  • Any lump you are not confident is a wart — sebaceous cysts, mast cell tumors, and other skin conditions can look similar and require different management

In dogs with severe cases — usually those on immunosuppressive medication or with widespread oral warts that are interfering with eating — veterinarians occasionally use specific interventions to speed resolution. But for the vast majority of otherwise healthy dogs, patience plus immune support does the job.

What the Bumps Are Really Saying

Those funny little cauliflower bumps are not nothing. They are a signal that your dog encountered a virus, and their immune system is now doing exactly what it is supposed to do. In most cases, they will come, they will persist for a few weeks, and they will disappear again with the immune system slightly stronger and better educated than it was before. Support the immune system with real food, a low-stress environment, and thoughtful integrative care, and the whole process usually resolves quietly on its own.

Keep an eye on them, take a picture now and then to track progress, and check in with your veterinarian — ideally one with an integrative or holistic bent — if anything looks off. But mostly, take a deep breath. Your dog is doing exactly what their body was built to do. Sometimes, the funny little bumps are just proof that everything is working.

Sources and References

  • 1,3,7,9 Front. Vet. Sci., 16 May 2023, Volume 10 - 2023
  • 2,4,6,8,10 Best Life 4 Pets, December 21, 2025
  • 5,11 Dogs Naturally Magazine, November 9, 2021

item.title: How Spaying and Neutering Influences Cancer and Disease Risk
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Studies show that spaying/neutering large and giant breed dogs increases the risk for many diseases, including several types of canine cancer
  • While animal health groups are reconsidering their position on automatic spays/neuters, animal welfare groups understandably remain firmly on the side of early spays or neuters for all shelter pets
  • A reasonable compromise may exist in broader use of sterilization procedures that do not remove the ovaries or testes
  • If you’re considering, for example, an ovary-sparing spay for a female dog or a vasectomy for a male, resources exist but aren’t widely available

item.title: Your Next Chapter Could Use a 4-Legged Sidekick
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Research shows adults 60 and older who own pets are 36% less likely to consider themselves lonely, with dog ownership also linked to lower blood pressure, better cardiovascular health, and improved cognitive function
  • Age matters less than lifestyle when choosing a dog — the right fit depends on exercise capability, training experience, living situation, financial readiness, and physical ability to walk and groom the dog
  • Easygoing breeds like Cavalier King Charles Spaniels, Shih Tzus, Pugs, French Bulldogs, Coton de Tulears, and Havanese suit seniors who prefer moderate exercise and lots of snuggle time
  • Active seniors may thrive with Bichon Frisés, Pembroke Welsh Corgis, English Cocker Spaniels, Dachshunds, Beagles, Boston Terriers, or Poodles — breeds that reward regular walks with better behavior at home
  • Consider adopting an adult or senior dog for a known personality and settled temperament, and always have a backup caregiver plan in place for the years ahead — many small breeds live 12 to 16 years or more

Life shifts as the years go by. Maybe the kids have long since moved out, and the house feels a little too quiet in the afternoons. Maybe you have retired, downsized, or just find yourself with more time on your hands and fewer built-in reasons to leave the front porch. There is a compelling body of research — and a lot of very happy pet parents in their 60s, 70s, and beyond — suggesting that this might be exactly the right chapter to bring a dog into your life.

Why a Dog May Be Just What You Need

The benefits of dog ownership stack up in ways that hit exactly what tends to slip in older age. In one study of adults 60 years or older,1 pet parents were 36% less likely to consider themselves lonely than non-pet parents. Dogs give you a reason to get up in the morning, a warm presence throughout the day, and a built-in conversation starter every time you take them out.2

Beyond the emotional piece, the health benefits are real. Dog ownership has been associated with lower stress levels, reduced blood pressure, better cardiovascular health, more consistent daily exercise, and even reduced risk of death due to heart disease.3

Petting a dog releases endorphins and can lower your heart rate on the spot. Walking a dog twice a day builds an exercise habit almost automatically. And the responsibility of caring for another living being — feeding, grooming, keeping an eye on their well-being — has been shown to help support cognitive function in older adults.4,5,6

For seniors living alone, in a quiet neighborhood, or in a senior community, a dog often becomes the single most consistent source of warmth, structure, and joy in the day. That is not sentimental language — it is what the research keeps showing.

Questions to Ask Yourself First

Age itself matters less than lifestyle and physical ability. A 68-year-old avid hiker and a 68-year-old who prefers reading in the recliner need very different dogs. Before you commit, run through a few honest questions:

  • How much daily exercise are you realistically up for — and enjoy?
  • Do you have experience training dogs, or would you want a breed that is easy to train?
  • Can you comfortably walk, lift, and groom the size of dog you are considering?
  • What is your living situation — house with a yard, apartment, senior community with a pet policy?
  • Do you travel often, and would you want your dog to come with you?
  • Will you have grandchildren visiting? A kid-friendly temperament matters.
  • Have you thought about who would care for your dog if you were unable — a family member, friend, or plan in place?
  • Can you comfortably cover the ongoing costs — food, veterinary care, grooming, boarding, supplies?

None of these are dealbreakers. They are just the practical realities that shape which breed will make you a very happy dog owner instead of an overwhelmed one.

Great Breeds for Easygoing Days

If your ideal afternoon involves a short walk followed by a snuggle on the couch, these breeds tend to be right at home. Most are small enough to lift comfortably, quiet enough for shared walls, and content with modest exercise, which makes them especially good matches for apartment living, senior communities, or anyone whose energy comes and goes throughout the day:7,8,9

  • Cavalier King Charles Spaniel — Probably the most-recommended breed for seniors. Warm, affectionate, gentle, and content with moderate exercise. Natural cuddler with soulful eyes.
  • Shih Tzu — A solid little dog (up to 16 pounds) bred as royal companions. Low exercise needs, friendly with grandchildren, and happy in an apartment.
  • Pug — Comical, affectionate, and low-key. Loves lounging with their humans (which means watching their weight matters). Playful with kids.
  • French Bulldog — The most popular AKC breed for several years running. Adaptable, quiet, and comfortable in smaller spaces.
  • Coton de Tulear — Cheerful, low-shedding, and easy to train. Adapts well to travel and can live 15 to 19 years, which is one of the longer lifespans in small breeds.
  • Havanese — The only breed native to Cuba. Quiet, cheerful, patient with children, and happy with short walks and lots of snuggle time.
  • Pomeranian — Tiny (under 7 pounds), smart, and easy to train. Content with indoor games and short walks.
  • Yorkshire Terrier — This breed is loving and outgoing but can be stubborn, so training experience helps.

Great Breeds for Active Seniors

If you are the retiree who is out at 6 a.m. for a walk in the park, thinking about hiking trips with the grandkids, or looking for a dog to keep pace with your energy, look at these breeds. They bring more energy, curiosity, and drive than the classic lap dogs, but they are still manageable for older adults who enjoy a real daily routine:10,11,12

  • Bichon Frisé — Curly-coated, hypoallergenic, playful, and lively. A great fit for active seniors who want a companion for both couch time and outings.
  • Pembroke Welsh Corgi — Around 30 pounds of muscle in a small package. Athletic and famously charming (Queen Elizabeth owned 30 of them), but they can be heavy shedders and need frequent brushing.
  • English Cocker Spaniel — Medium-sized, lively, quick learner, and happy with a couple of 30-minute walks a day. Good traveler and loves being wherever you are. This breed does need careful grooming to manage their silky coat and allergy prone skin.
  • Dachshund — Small but spirited, comes in standard and miniature sizes with three coat types. Low grooming needs; short walks are ideal because they are prone to back problems, and this is not a breed made for jumping on and off the bed or navigating steep stairs.
  • Italian Greyhound — Playful, graceful, and lap-loving. Requires regular exercise and appreciates a sweater in chilly weather.
  • Beagle — Friendly, energetic, and motivating for owners who want a dog that will insist on daily walks. This is a breed known for baying, so noise can be a limitation.
  • Boston Terrier — Affectionate, adaptable, and trainable. Great for small apartments. Some respiratory limits in hot weather.
  • Poodle (Standard, Miniature, or Toy) — Intelligent, trainable, hypoallergenic, and adaptable to almost any living situation.

Should You Get a Puppy or an Adult Dog?

This is one of the bigger decisions. Puppies are adorable, but they are also a full-time commitment for the first year or so — housebreaking, chewing, midnight potty breaks, obedience training, and enough energy to test anyone's patience. If you are up for it, a puppy grows into exactly the dog you shape.

For most older adults, an adult or senior dog is often a better fit. They come already housebroken and leash-trained, their personalities are settled so you know what you are getting, and their energy tends to be more predictable. Adopting an older dog from a shelter or breed-specific rescue also gives a home to a dog who needs one — and older dogs are frequently overlooked in shelters despite being some of the loveliest companions available.

Adopting Versus Buying

While reputable breeders can help match you with the right temperament, screen for breed-specific health issues, and answer questions about lifespan and care over the years, it is highly recommended to check your local animal shelter first. Local shelters are full of loving, pure and mixed breeds pets that are waiting for their forever home. Plus, their personalities are already known, and many of them are the exact easygoing lap-dog temperaments that suit older adults perfectly.

In addition, make sure to spend time with the dog before committing. Personality varies within every breed. The right fit is not just about breed characteristics — it is about the specific dog in front of you.

Planning for the Long Haul

A responsible piece of getting a dog at this stage of life is thinking beyond today. Small dogs commonly live 12 to 16 years — some longer. Consider:

  • Who would care for the dog if you had a health event or were unable for a stretch?
  • Is there a family member, neighbor, or friend committed to helping if needed?
  • If you might move into senior living or assisted care, are you looking at pet-friendly options? Many facilities allow pets but have size, weight, or type restrictions.
  • Financial planning for veterinary care, grooming, boarding, and supplies over the dog's lifetime.
  • A simple written plan for what happens to your dog if you are unable to care for them, shared with the person who would step in.

None of this should stop you. It is just good planning, and it makes the dog's future secure regardless of what happens.

A Companion for the Chapter Ahead

The research keeps landing in the same place. Dog ownership in later life is associated with less loneliness, more physical activity, better mood, sharper cognition, lower blood pressure, and a richer daily experience. And beyond the studies, there is the simple daily reality — a warm body curled up next to you in the evening, a wagging tail meeting you at the door, and someone who genuinely delights in every small thing you do together.

Whether you pick a Cavalier King Charles Spaniel for lap-dog snuggles, a Pembroke Welsh Corgi for morning walks with attitude, or a mixed-breed rescue whose story finds you when you visit the shelter, the right dog can turn what might be a quieter chapter of life into one of the fullest. Talk to your doctor if you have health questions, talk to your vet about which breeds fit your situation, and talk to shelters and rescues about who is waiting for you. Your next chapter could genuinely use a four-legged sidekick. And there is a very good chance one is already looking for you.

Sources and References

  • 1 Aging Ment Health. 2014; 18(3): 394–399
  • 2,4,9,12 American Kennel Club, August 17, 2026
  • 3 Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and OutcomesVolume 12, Number 10, October 8, 2019
  • 5,8,11 LTC News, June 13, 2023
  • 6 Sci Rep. 2023 Sep 7;13:14738. doi: 10.1038/s41598-023-41813-y
  • 7,10 Good Housekeeping, September 9, 2026

While reputable breeders can help match you with the right temperament, screen for breed-specific health issues, and answer questions about lifespan and care over the years, it is highly recommended to check your local animal shelter first. Local shelters are full of loving, pure and mixed breeds pets that are waiting for their forever home. Plus, their personalities are already known, and many of them are the exact easygoing lap-dog temperaments that suit older adults perfectly.

In addition, make sure to spend time with the dog before committing. Personality varies within every breed. The right fit is not just about breed characteristics — it is about the specific dog in front of you.

Planning for the Long Haul

A responsible piece of getting a dog at this stage of life is thinking beyond today. Small dogs commonly live 12 to 16 years — some longer. Consider:

  • Who would care for the dog if you had a health event or were unable for a stretch?
  • Is there a family member, neighbor, or friend committed to helping if needed?
  • If you might move into senior living or assisted care, are you looking at pet-friendly options? Many facilities allow pets but have size, weight, or type restrictions.
  • Financial planning for veterinary care, grooming, boarding, and supplies over the dog's lifetime.
  • A simple written plan for what happens to your dog if you are unable to care for them, shared with the person who would step in.

None of this should stop you. It is just good planning, and it makes the dog's future secure regardless of what happens.

A Companion for the Chapter Ahead

The research keeps landing in the same place. Dog ownership in later life is associated with less loneliness, more physical activity, better mood, sharper cognition, lower blood pressure, and a richer daily experience. And beyond the studies, there is the simple daily reality — a warm body curled up next to you in the evening, a wagging tail meeting you at the door, and someone who genuinely delights in every small thing you do together.

Whether you pick a Cavalier King Charles Spaniel for lap-dog snuggles, a Pembroke Welsh Corgi for morning walks with attitude, or a mixed-breed rescue whose story finds you when you visit the shelter, the right dog can turn what might be a quieter chapter of life into one of the fullest. Talk to your doctor if you have health questions, talk to your vet about which breeds fit your situation, and talk to shelters and rescues about who is waiting for you. Your next chapter could genuinely use a four-legged sidekick. And there is a very good chance one is already looking for you.
